title: The Casual Observer: Low-Activity Twitter Users as Arbiters of (Mis)Information in the War in Ukraine
screen_reason: Behavioural analysis of 117,144,527 tweets from 10,020,547 Twitter accounts matching 'ukraine'/'kyiv' over the first 150 days of the 2022 invasion. Links were matched against a 378-domain Media Bias/Fact Check list of low-credibility sources, and the paper reports that 321,806 users (3.2%) shared links to misinformation sources. That is an observed share of users who shared misinformation from platform data, i.e. SHARING (actor_share), with an explicit denominator.

estimates.country: Global (Twitter's global live streaming API; no country restriction; top shared domains dominated by English-language outlets)
estimates.date: February 25 to July 24, 2022 (first 150 days of the 2022 Russia-Ukraine conflict)
estimates.measure_type: % of Twitter accounts tweeting about the war in Ukraine that shared at least one link to a low-credibility (misinformation) source
estimates.denominator: 10,020,547 Twitter accounts appearing in a collection of 117,144,527 tweets captured live on the keywords 'ukraine' and 'kyiv', 25 February - 24 July 2022
estimates.definition: The account shared at least one link whose top-level domain matched a manually compiled list of 378 'low credibility' source domains from Media Bias/Fact Check - the 'questionable' and 'conspiracy-pseudoscience' categories - following Pierri et al. (2022)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'The misinformation sources were defined according to the classifications of Media Bias/Fact Check (MB/FC), which is a website that rates the accuracy and bias of news sources ... a list of what are classified as “low credibility” sources was compiled; these include what Van Zandt calls questionable sources and conspiracy-pseudoscience sources.'
estimates.source_quote: Of the 10,020,547 total users in the data, 321,806 (or 3.2%) shared links to misinformation sources; however, only 19,624 of the misinformation sharers are casual users (out of 4,962,233 total casual users.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 'A list of 378 misinformation sources and their associated domains was compiled from MB/FC manually. URLs and domains within the tweets were then extracted using built-in tools of the DMI-TCAT in combination with Regex extractions. The top-level domains of the URLs were then compared to the list of misinformation sources.' Ground truth is therefore a third-party source-reliability rating (Media Bias/Fact Check), applied at domain level. No validation, coder agreement or accuracy statistic is reported for the list or the matching.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data used in this study consisted of 117 million tweets collected from Twitter in real-time using the keywords “ukraine” and “kyiv”.
estimates.notes: Breadth is left empty per the schema rule for source-level domain lists. IMPORTANT DENOMINATOR NOTE for the adjudicator: the denominator is ALL accounts in the keyword collection, including the very many that never shared any link at all, so 3.2% is not the share of link-sharing users who shared a low-credibility link - it is the share of all Ukraine-tweeting accounts. Note also that the paper never reports the share of TWEETS that carried misinformation links, only the share of accounts, so no content_share row is available. denom_scope=topical because the population is defined by a two-keyword war corpus, not a general population.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The casual-user figure - '19,624 of the misinformation sharers are casual users (out of 4,962,233 total casual users. In other words, only 0.39% of casual users shared misinformation' - is the paper's headline but was NOT written as a row. Reason: 'casual user' is defined as an account that tweeted exactly once in the collection, so its misinformation-sharing rate is mechanically bounded by that single tweet; the comparison is an activity-level artefact rather than a population estimate, and the author concedes as much ('casual users by definition share fewer tweets in general, so this lower proportion could be due to their general lower levels of activity'). Flagged here in full so an adjudicator can add it if the review wants activity-stratified sharing rows. The complementary non-casual rate is not printed and could only be obtained by subtracting across categories, which R8 forbids. 2) CONCENTRATION judgement call: 'casual users, meaning those who only appear once in the data, make up 49.5% of the userbase (4,962,233 users out of 10,020,547), and produced 4.2% of the total tweets (4,962,233 tweets out of 117,144,527)'. This has the shape of a concentration statistic (a user group as % of users + their share of activity) and both numbers are verbatim, but it was NOT coded CONCENTRATION because (a) it describes the concentration of TWEETING IN GENERAL, not of misinformation exposure or sharing, and (b) it is stated for the BOTTOM activity group; turning it into a top-group statement (the other 50.5% of users produced 95.8% of tweets) would be a complement computed by the extractor, which R8 forbids. An adjudicator who reads CONCENTRATION as covering general-activity concentration could add a row with conc_group_pct 49.5, conc_share_pct 4.2, conc_unit user, conc_dimension sharing, conc_group_label 'casual (single-tweet) users'. 3) Table 2 gives the composition of misinformation tweets by form (non-casual users: retweet 0.66, comment-no-mention 0.25, via 0.04, reply 0.03, mention 0.01; casual users: retweet 0.68, comment 0.25, via 0.05, reply 0.02, mention 0.01). These are shares of misinformation tweets by tweet type, not prevalence of misinformation, so no rows. 4) Top-domain shares (YouTube 11% of tweets with URLs, Reuters 5%, New York Times 5%, BBC 4%, Guardian 3.8%, Washington Post 3.1%, CNN 2.8%, Telegram 2.5%, Wall Street Journal 1.6%, Associated Press 1.4%) are mainstream outlets, not misinformation sources, so no row. 5) The logistic regression (n = 200,000 random sample) reports odds ratios only, and the author notes it 'has very low sensitivity, successfully identifying only 14.3% of the misinformation sharers'. 6) '10% of users contribute 80% of the tweets' is a Pew statistic cited from Wojcik & Hughes (2019), not this paper's data - excluded under R8, and it would otherwise have been a tempting CONCENTRATION row.

rob.design: Observational analysis of platform trace data. Frame: Twitter's global live streaming API captured via DMI-TCAT on two keywords, 'ukraine' and 'kyiv', 25 February - 24 July 2022 (the first 150 days of the invasion), yielding 117,144,527 tweets from 10,020,547 accounts, loaded into Google BigQuery; the collection includes tweets later deleted. No probability sampling and no response rate; the corpus is defined by two English-language keywords, which will under-capture non-English and non-keyword war discourse. Misinformation exposure measured by URL matching only: the top-level domains of extracted URLs were compared with a manually compiled list of 378 low-credibility domains taken from Media Bias/Fact Check ('questionable' plus 'conspiracy-pseudoscience'), following Pierri et al. (2022). No inter-coder reliability, no validation of the domain list, and no claim-level verification; a link is counted regardless of whether the sharer endorsed or debunked it. 'Casual users' are defined by an explicitly acknowledged artificial threshold (exactly one tweet in the collection), and the author notes these are not true lurkers. A logistic regression on a random subsample (n = 200,000) tested activity predictors; it was significant (chi2(6) = 17094.15, p < .001) but had very low sensitivity (14.3%), and the author concludes 'user activity level is not a good predictor of misinformation sharing'. Single-author study; no ethics statement reported.
rob.item6_quote: The misinformation sources were defined according to the classifications of Media Bias/Fact Check (MB/FC), which is a website that rates the accuracy and bias of news sources (Van Zandt, 2022). Drawing on Pierri et al. (2022), a list of what are classified as “low credibility” sources was compiled; these include what Van Zandt calls questionable sources and conspiracy-pseudoscience sources. A list of 378 misinformation sources and their associated domains was compiled from MB/FC manually.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 10,020,547 total users in the data, 321,806 (or 3.2%) shared links to misinformation sources; however, only 19,624 of the misinformation sharers are casual users (out of 4,962,233 total casual users. In other words, only 0.39% of casual users shared misinformation.
